sentences.text: The animal possessed a large, slender head measuring 13.3 centimeters in cranial length and 11.7 centimeters in mandibular length.
Its skull featured a slightly bent jugal bone creating a curved margin below the eye socket, while the bone was notably narrow compared to other relatives.
The top of the braincase resulted from fused frontal and parietal bones curving sharply downward, and the back included a short, wide basisphenoid with a U-shaped notch.
Additionally, the atlas and axis vertebrae were fused together, though a visible suture line remained.
The jaws held approximately 152 long, needle-like teeth that were tightly packed and projected outward.
In each jaw, the first tooth was about half the length of the second tooth.
When the jaws closed, these interlocking teeth formed a comb-like structure designed for filter-feeding.
This creature holds the distinction of being the oldest known ctenochasmatid and the first filter-feeding pterosaur discovered in the Tiaojishan Formation.
The genus name combines "Liao," a shortened form of Liaoning, with the Greek word dactylos meaning "finger," while the species name primus refers to its age relative to other ctenochasmatids.
The genus Liaodactylus was described by Zhou et al. in 2017.
Only one specimen is known, the holotype PMOL-AP00031, which is housed at the Palaeontological Museum of Liaoning.
The fossil was found in outcrops located about 500 meters west of Daxishan village in Jianchang, Liaoning, China.
As an adaptation for filter-feeding, the animal had approximately 150 teeth arranged very closely together like a comb.
Liaodactylus represents the first filter-feeding pterosaur found in the Yanliao biota.
Liaodactylus is classified as a filter-feeding ctenochasmatid pterosaur from the Jurassic of China.
Zhou and colleagues assigned the animal to the family Ctenochasmatidae in 2017 based on a phylogenetic analysis.
Phylogenetic analysis places Liaodactylus closest to Ctenochasma, sharing similar jaw-to-skull ratios and outward-angled teeth.
Liaodactylus lived during the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic, approximately 161.8 to 159.5 million years ago.
The animal inhabited a forested woodland environment containing conifers, cycads, and ferns.
The climate where it lived was cool, temperate, wet, and seasonal, with a mean temperature below 15 °C.

Liaodactylus is known from the Tiaojishan Formation, which along with the older Haifanggou Formation forms the Yanliao biota, a diverse and well-preserved association of Jurassic animals containing at least 40 species.
A 2023 study proposed that the Liaodactylus fossils belong to the Haifanggou Formation rather than the Tiaojishan Formation.
